query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ formation of a coherent, ~50 nm-thick protective oxide layer on the HEA surface reduces adhesive wear by mitigating direct metal-to-metal contact during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: The baseline HEA coating features minimal preformed oxide, resulting in direct metallic contact with the opposing sliding surface.
generation.intervention: Thermally pre-age the coating by exposing it to a controlled, oxygen-rich environment (e.g., annealing in air at 750 °C for 30 minutes) to develop a continuous, protective oxide layer enriched in Cr, Cu, or Fe.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding (approximately 800 °C) in an oxygen-containing atmosphere, where controlled oxidation kinetics allow formation of a stable oxide film.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous oxide film (~50 nm thick) that forms on the HEA surface and remains adherent during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide layer acts as a low-friction barrier that minimizes adhesive interactions by preventing direct metallic contact and distributing contact stresses uniformly.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized coating, when tested under the same sliding conditions as a non-oxidized sample, will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and decreased wear volume, with post-test analyses revealing an intact oxide scale.
generation.baseline: A HEA coating tested in an inert or low-oxygen environment, lacking a continuous protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is valid if the oxide layer remains intact and does not spall during cyclic sliding, and if the substrate does not adversely affect oxide layer formation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal oxide composition, exact thickness, and long-term stability under sustained cyclic sliding require further experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one pre-oxidized via annealing in air at 750 °C for 30 minutes and one maintained in a low-oxygen environment. Subject both samples to high-temperature sliding tests at 800 °C and perform surface analysis (XPS/EDS) before and after testing.
measurements: Friction coefficient and wear rate during sliding
Oxide layer thickness and composition via XPS/EDS
Surface morphology and evidence of spallation via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized sample does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in wear resistance or if the protective oxide layer is absent or degrades during sliding, the hypothesis is refuted.

The thermal-exposure caused the ferrite grain-size of the steel coating, has revealed that interlamellar-spacing as well as pearlite-formation has made contributions towards this transformation. These protective-shielding layers or barrier-coatings are crucial for enhancing the characteristics of resistance to corrosion as well as resistance to wear. Figure 13a–d has unveiled the optical microscopic view of the cladding samples of SS-304 coating with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu before and after thermal exposure in the air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C. The Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA is coated onto the SS-304 substrate using a microwave cladding process, which initially interacts by melting and fusing the alloy to the substrate. At 800 °C, alloying elements from the cladding composition can diffuse into the substrate, and the substrate's constituents can diffuse into the cladding. cited_evidence.text: Figure 16 shows the SEM wear morphology and EDS spectrum analysis of HVOF coating under different heat-treatment conditions. The middle of two red dotted lines is the wear region. The three-body wear between the coating, counter-wear ball and quartz sand in the drilling fluid is still the main wear mechanism. Since the HVOF coating is a traditional layered structure of thermal spraying, the peeling phenomenon is more obvious than that of the CS coating.
